project.name: wasm3
project.fuzz_target: platforms/app/main.c (`wasm3` CLI loading the saved file witness)

staged_source_snapshot.description: Stage 01 reproduced against this staged vulnerable wasm3 checkout. All cited file/line anchors come from that saved source tree.

bug_description.original: A global-buffer-overflow in m3_compile.c: Compile_BlockStatements (opcode decoding) causes an out-of-bounds read from the global opcode table c_operationsFC. While compiling/parsing block expressions (seen via Parse_InitExpr / ParseSection_Data), an opcode index can exceed the c_operationsFC bounds and read 8 bytes past the array, leading to crashes or disclosure of adjacent memory.
bug_description.normalized: The exact staged witness is the 108-byte file `gt_results/secbench_oss_wasm3.ossfuzz-42495624/poc` (sha256 `9ed0703af7205f1ec8c5df09a1c07de526a8d1aa886fcdf6301825fdec2d23cf`). Static inspection of that file shows a valid wasm magic/version header (`00 61 73 6d 01 00 00 00`) followed immediately by section id `0x0b`, so `m3_ParseModule()` dispatches into `ParseSection_Data()`. For each data-segment initializer, `Parse_InitExpr()` creates a parser-side `M3Compilation` over the attacker-controlled init-expression bytes and calls `Compile_BlockStatements()` to walk until an `end` opcode. The exact witness contains no `0xFC` bytes anywhere, so `Read_opcode()` cannot construct an extended opcode on the crashing path: the later bad dispatch stays on `GetOpInfo()`'s ordinary-opcode arm (`opcode >> 8 == 0x00`) and performs the unchecked lookup `&c_operations[opcode]`. Because that helper does not prove `opcode < M3_COUNT_OF(c_operations)`, it can return a non-NULL pointer outside the real table; `_throwif(m3Err_unknownOpcode, opinfo == NULL)` therefore does not reject it, and line 2210 immediately dereferences `opinfo->compiler`, producing the saved AddressSanitizer global-buffer-overflow in `Compile_BlockStatements`. The public default crash trace names the faulting address relative to `c_operationsFC`, but that is a layout-specific description of where the out-of-range ordinary-opcode pointer lands among nearby globals in that build, not evidence that this witness took the `0xFC` branch. The local Stage 01 ASan rebuild reaches the same source line and parser path and likewise reports the same unchecked opcode-table dereference with different adjacent-global naming. The patch fixes the broader source-level obligation by moving `GetOpInfo()` into `m3_compile.c` and adding bounds checks for both the ordinary and `0xFC` opcode tables. Stage 02 did not execute the fixed build.

source.description: First project-side materialization point for the vulnerability-relevant data: `Parse_InitExpr()` wraps the current attacker-controlled data-segment initializer bytes in a temporary `M3Compilation` and seeds the byte-walk state that `Compile_BlockStatements()` will consume.
source.value_from: The saved witness is the exact 108-byte file `gt_results/secbench_oss_wasm3.ossfuzz-42495624/poc` (sha256 `9ed0703af7205f1ec8c5df09a1c07de526a8d1aa886fcdf6301825fdec2d23cf`). Its first eight bytes are the standard wasm magic/version header and its first section byte is `0x0b`, so the staged crash path reaches `ParseSection_Data()` and hands a data-segment init-expression byte stream into this initializer.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer sink. This is the first dereference of the unchecked opcode-info pointer returned by `GetOpInfo()`.
sink.note: Both saved ASan traces fault at `Compile_BlockStatements` line 2210 on a read of size 8. For this exact witness the unchecked pointer comes from the ordinary `c_operations` lookup, not the `0xFC` table. The public trace's `c_operationsFC` wording reflects where that out-of-range ordinary-opcode pointer lands in one build's global layout, while the local Stage 01 trace reaches the same line through `Parse_InitExpr -> ParseSection_Data` and labels different neighboring globals.

root_cause.description: Witness-specific root cause. On the crashing path `GetOpInfo()` stays on the ordinary-opcode arm and uses the attacker-derived opcode directly as a `c_operations` index with no bounds check.
root_cause.note: The exact staged witness contains no `0xFC` bytes, so this sample never reaches the extended-opcode arm. The fix still matters more broadly because the patched helper adds bounds checks for both the ordinary and `0xFC` opcode tables before returning a pointer.

tainted_value_origin.description: This helper decodes the current init-expression bytes into the opcode value that `GetOpInfo()` later turns into an unchecked table pointer. Because the exact witness contains no `0xFC` bytes, the crashing path keeps the single-byte ordinary opcode unchanged instead of widening it into an extended opcode.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: Step 1 seeds `o->wasm` from the current data-segment init-expression stream, and the saved crash stack proves that stream is being consumed under `ParseSection_Data -> Parse_InitExpr -> Compile_BlockStatements` when line 2210 faults. Static inspection of the saved 108-byte witness finds no `0xFC` bytes at any offset, so this GT can rule out the extended-opcode branch even though the staged artifacts do not log the exact later file offset of the crashing byte.

parser_admitted.description: Sample-specific admission point. After `m3_ParseModule()` accepts the wasm header and section ordering, section id `0x0b` resolves to `ParseSection_Data`, and this dispatch enters the data-section parser that later invokes `Parse_InitExpr()` on the crashing initializer.

coarse_trace.summary: The CLI loads the saved 108-byte witness, `m3_ParseModule()` accepts the wasm header, and section dispatch reaches the data section.
Data-section parsing captures the current initializer byte stream and wraps it in a temporary `M3Compilation` for `Compile_BlockStatements()`.
A later walk over the malformed initializer decodes a single-byte ordinary opcode, stays off the `0xFC` extended-opcode arm, and uses that byte as an unchecked `c_operations` index.
The null-only unknown-opcode guard lets the out-of-range pointer pass, and line 2210 dereferences `opinfo->compiler`, producing the ASan global-buffer-overflow.

fine_trace.note: Source. `Parse_InitExpr()` materializes a temporary `M3Compilation` over the current data-segment initializer. The nearby comment says this path "just walks the wasm bytecode to find the end", so later `Compile_BlockStatements()` iterations read directly from the attacker-supplied init-expression bytes in `compilation.wasm`.

A later crashing iteration of the init-expression walk decodes the next attacker-controlled byte from `o->wasm` into local variable `opcode` and stores it to `*o_value`. The exact 108-byte witness contains no `0xFC` bytes anywhere, so this path never takes the widening branch that would build an extended opcode; the next step therefore receives an ordinary single-byte opcode (`opcode >> 8 == 0x00`). Earlier noncrashing iterations and recursive call plumbing are omitted because they only advance the same byte stream to this later decode site.

Root cause. Because step 2 never builds an extended opcode for this witness, `GetOpInfo()` dispatches on the ordinary-opcode arm and returns `&c_operations[opcode]`. That lookup uses the attacker-derived byte directly as an array index and does not check `opcode < M3_COUNT_OF(c_operations)`, so an out-of-range opcode yields a non-NULL pointer outside the real table.

The only guard after `GetOpInfo()` rejects a NULL pointer, not an out-of-range one. Because step 3 returns a non-NULL pointer value even when it aliases memory beyond the opcode table, this check succeeds and control falls through to the dereference site.
Sink. `Compile_BlockStatements()` dereferences the unchecked pointer from step 3 to read its `compiler` field. That first field read is the saved AddressSanitizer global-buffer-overflow at line 2210.

cross_validation.sink_matches_crash: Yes. Both saved ASan traces report a read of size 8 in `Compile_BlockStatements` at `source/m3_compile.c:2210`, and fine-trace step 5 is that exact dereference. The public trace names the address relative to `c_operationsFC`, but the witness-specific causal chain still reaches that sink through the ordinary `c_operations` lookup in step 3.
cross_validation.trace_consistent_with_stack: Yes. The local Stage 01 stack is `Compile_BlockStatements -> CompileBlock -> Compile_If -> Compile_BlockStatements -> Parse_InitExpr -> ParseSection_Data -> ParseModuleSection -> m3_ParseModule -> repl_load -> main`; the fine trace models the same admitted data-section initializer path, collapsing only noncrashing earlier loop/recursive iterations that merely advance to the later opcode decode.
cross_validation.tainted_value_reaches_sink: Yes. Step 1 seeds `compilation.wasm` from the attacker-controlled initializer bytes, step 2 decodes a later single-byte opcode and rules out the `0xFC` widening branch for this witness, step 3 uses that byte as an unchecked `c_operations` index, and step 5 dereferences the resulting pointer at the ASan sink.

poc.trigger: Run `build/wasm3` on the saved 108-byte wasm witness so module parsing reaches `ParseSection_Data()`, `Parse_InitExpr()` walks a malformed data-segment initializer, and `Compile_BlockStatements()` dereferences an unchecked opcode-table pointer at line 2210.

format.name: raw WebAssembly binary file
format.contract: The verified trigger is only the exact staged 108-byte witness file `poc` with sha256 `9ed0703af7205f1ec8c5df09a1c07de526a8d1aa886fcdf6301825fdec2d23cf`. Static inspection confirms only that it begins with valid wasm magic/version bytes and enters the data-section init-expression parser path. The saved artifacts do not log the exact later crashing opcode byte or its file offset inside the malformed initializer, so the contract should not be generalized beyond this exact witness.

evidence_limitations: The saved artifacts do not expose the exact later opcode value or byte offset that produced the invalid `GetOpInfo()` index; identifying that offset would require runtime logging or separate probing, which Stage 02 does not perform.

The public default crash trace attributes the invalid read to `c_operationsFC`, while the local Stage 01 ASan rebuild reaches the same line and parser path in a differently laid-out image and ASan reports nearby globals instead. This GT therefore anchors the source-level root cause at the shared unchecked `GetOpInfo()` index rather than claiming a build-specific global-layout detail.
